The current study observed this interaction between tones and reaction times, while also going beyond this and taking into account another dimension, word meaning. Though in English there is no dependence on tone in determining semantic meaning to cause confusion, there are other aspects of the language which can still create problems with understanding, such as homophones, words which are pronounced the same but have different meanings.  For monolingual speakers of English, homophones can generally be distinguished only by context within a sentence or situation.  The objective of this study was to observe whether Mandarin-English bilinguals take the skill acquired in Mandarin of relying on tones to differentiate meaning in words and automatically apply it to their interpretation of English words.  It was hypothesized that Mandarin-English bilinguals would choose a homophone that is presented in a tone which matches the tone of the Mandarin translation of the word.  English monolinguals, on the other hand, were expected to choose either version of the English homophone at random.  Gaining information about how individuals process language, particularly how bilinguals do this, provides insight into how bilinguals manage their languages and to what extent each language influences processing and comprehension in the other.  It also has implications for how tonal-language bilinguals learn and perceive other languages that do not have a tonal aspect.

The study followed a 2×2 factorial design, with two between-subject independent factors, group and tone. Group has two levels: 1) monolingual English; and 2) bilingual Mandarin-English.  Tone also has two levels: 1) the Mandarin tone of one translation of the homophone; and 2) the Mandarin tone of the other translation of the homophone.  The four dependent variables are 1) word choice, 2) first reaction time, 3) second reaction time, and 4) third reaction time.  The first, second, and third reaction times measure 1) the time required for auditory recognition of the word, 2) written production of the word, and 3) oral production of a simple sentence containing the word, respectively.

Participants in this experiment included 20 balanced (equally proficient in both languages) Mandarin-English bilinguals (eight males and 12 females; mean age = 21.550, SD = 5.300) and 20 English monolinguals (nine males and 11 females; mean age = 19.800, SD = 1.200).  All Mandarin-English participants were native Mandarin speakers who learned Mandarin either prior to, or concurrently with, English and were highly proficient in both languages; proficiencies in speaking, listening, and reading were assessed through self-reports using the Language Experience and Proficiency Questionnaire (LEAP-Q).⁸  All monolingual participants were also given the LEAP-Q to assess their self-rated proficiencies in English, as well as to exclude any participants who might have any prior exposure to or knowledge of Mandarin or other tonal languages.  See Tables 1 and 2 for participant information.

The stimuli used in the experiment were 20 single-syllable English homophones which had single syllable Mandarin translations with different tones for both homophone definitions.  These homophones were checked for word frequency using the CELEX lexical database.⁹  Homophone pairs that showed too great a difference in frequency within the pair were discarded, since the effect of word frequency could possibly confound the results, with high frequency words being chosen preferentially over low-frequency words due to familiarity rather than supra-segmental influences.  These homophones, along with 55 non-homophone filler words, were recorded by an English monolingual speaker with no accent or speech disorder.  These words were manipulated using Praat computer software in order to superimpose the appropriate Mandarin tone, using guidelines established in a previous research study.¹⁰ Duration and amplitude were also normalized using Praat.  Each homophone was presented in a Mandarin tone that corresponded to the tone of one of the translations of the homophone, and the filler words were presented in random tones balanced between the four possible tones.  The stimuli were presented in one tone for half the participants (Block 1) and the other tone for the other half of the participants (Block 2) in a random order, using Superlab computer software.

In addition, two pairs were excluded for similar reasons, with one word out of the pair being chosen only once out of all 40 participants (i.e., blue/blew; raise/rays), suggesting that, even after controlling for frequency, frequency and familiarity, rather than tone, affect word choice.  After taking these eight pairs out, there were 12 homophone pairs remaining for the final analyses.  Table 3 lists these experimental pairs and additional information.

Prior to the experiment, participants were asked to complete the LEAP-Q¹¹ as a pre-screening process for participant selection.  This was to ensure that participants had the desired proficiency levels in Mandarin and English (for bilinguals) or no prior exposure to Mandarin or tonal languages (for monolinguals).  After providing written consent, participants were placed in a quiet room in front of a computer and microphone and were provided with a blank numbered sheet of paper and a pen.  Instructions given to participants prior to the experiment were to listen to the word, press a button to indicate that they understood the word, write down the word that they heard, press a button to indicate that they were finished writing, think of and record a simple sentence using the word in context, and press a button to indicate they were ready to move to the next word.

The results were coded as correct or incorrect for all the stimuli, homophones and fillers, based on whether the word written by the participant was the word presented.
